title: Linked List Design Problems
summary: Classic system-style design questions — random-pointer copying, list flattening, digit-wise arithmetic — built entirely on the pointer-manipulation skills from earlier in this group.

slides.markdown:
This topic is where the earlier pointer-manipulation skills in this group — reversal, fast/slow traversal, merging — get combined into small design problems rather than single algorithms.

Three of the most-asked list-anchored design questions live here: copying a list where nodes have an extra pointer to an arbitrary other node, flattening a multilevel list into one level, and adding two numbers stored digit-by-digit as lists. None of them are conceptually new; each is a fresh way of composing techniques you already have.

(The doubly-linked-list mechanics behind an LRU cache — a design question that's arguably the most-asked of all — live in the `hashing` group, alongside the hashmap half of that design.)

slides.sectionTitle: Why linked lists anchor design questions
slides.markdown:
Interviewers reach for list-based design problems because they force you to reason about **pointer invariants under construction** — the list is being built or copied while you're still deciding what its final shape looks like, unlike a single-pass algorithm on an already-complete structure.

That's a genuinely different skill from traversal or reversal: you have to keep track of a mapping between old and new structures (copying), or of multiple levels of pointers simultaneously (flattening), or of state that carries across node boundaries (carry in digit addition). Getting the pointer bookkeeping right under that extra complexity is what separates a clean solution from a tangled one.

slides.sectionTitle: Copying a list with random pointers
slides.subTitle: The interleave-then-split trick
slides.markdown:
Each node has a `next` pointer plus a `random` pointer that can point to *any* node in the list (or null). Copying it correctly means every copied node's `random` must point to the **copy** of the right original node, not the original itself — but you don't know all the copies exist yet while you're still walking the list once.

The O(1)-extra-space trick: **interleave** a copy of each node directly after its original (`A → A' → B → B' → …`). Now every node's copy is reachable as `node.next`, so you can set each copy's `random` as `node.random.next` (the copy of whatever the original pointed to) in a second pass — without ever needing a lookup table. A third pass **splits** the interleaved list back into two separate lists, original and copy.

| | Hashmap approach | Interleaving trick |
|---|---|---|
| Passes needed | 2 | 3 |
| Extra space | O(n) map of original→copy | O(1) |
| Code complexity | simpler to write and explain | more pointer bookkeeping |
| When it wins | space isn't constrained | O(1) extra space is required |

The hashmap version is easier to reason about: first pass creates all copies and records `original → copy` in a map; second pass sets each copy's `next` and `random` by looking up the map. It's the answer to give first if space isn't explicitly constrained — it's harder to get wrong under interview pressure.

The interleaving trick is what you reach for when asked to do it in O(1) extra space — worth naming both, and picking based on what the interviewer actually asked for rather than defaulting to the cleverer one.

slides.sectionTitle: Flattening a multilevel doubly linked list
slides.markdown:
Some nodes have a `child` pointer to a separate doubly linked sublist; flattening means splicing every child list into the main list, in place, at the position of the node that owns it.

```python
def flatten(head):
    curr = head
    while curr:
        if curr.child:
            next_node = curr.next
            child_tail = curr.child
            while child_tail.next:      # find end of child list
                child_tail = child_tail.next
            curr.next = curr.child      # splice child in
            curr.child.prev = curr
            curr.child = None
            child_tail.next = next_node # reattach the rest
            if next_node:
                next_node.prev = child_tail
        curr = curr.next
    return head
```

The walk to find `child_tail` means this isn't strictly O(n) in the naive worst case (deeply nested single-child chains can make it O(n²)) — worth flagging if asked about complexity, along with the fact that a recursive version handling one level of nesting per call has the same characteristic.

slides.sectionTitle: Adding two numbers as linked lists
slides.subTitle: Digit by digit with carry
slides.markdown:
Two numbers are stored as lists of digits (often least-significant-digit first). Adding them means walking both simultaneously, summing corresponding digits plus a running carry, and building a new list of result digits.

```python
def add_two_numbers(l1, l2):
    dummy = tail = Node(0)
    carry = 0
    while l1 or l2 or carry:
        x = l1.val if l1 else 0
        y = l2.val if l2 else 0
        total = x + y + carry
        carry, digit = divmod(total, 10)
        tail.next = Node(digit)
        tail = tail.next
        l1 = l1.next if l1 else None
        l2 = l2.next if l2 else None
    return dummy.next
```

The loop condition `l1 or l2 or carry` is the detail people miss: the shorter list running out doesn't end the computation if a carry is still propagating (e.g., 999 + 1 needs a fourth output digit after both input lists are exhausted).

```python
# BUG: stops as soon as both lists are exhausted, ignoring a trailing carry
while l1 or l2:
    ...
# missing: append one more digit if carry is still nonzero here
```

Once both input lists run out, a nonzero carry means the sum has one more digit than either input — classic case: adding 5 + 5 (each a single-node list holding 5) should produce the two-digit result "0, 1" (i.e., 10), but a loop that stops the moment both lists are empty drops that final carry digit and returns just "0".

The fix is including `carry` itself in the loop's continuation condition, as shown in the previous slide, rather than treating it as something checked only *inside* the loop body. This is the single most common bug in this exact problem — always trace through a same-length, all-9s input by hand before calling the solution done.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading these problems for their real skill
slides.markdown:
All three design problems in this topic reward the same instinct: **decompose into known primitives instead of inventing something bespoke.** Random-pointer copying is a mapping problem solved either with a hash map or with a clever in-place encoding; flattening is repeated splicing; digit addition is a simulation with careful loop-termination logic.

What interviewers are actually grading, beyond "does the code run," is whether you can hold multiple pointer relationships in your head simultaneously without losing track of one while updating another — which is exactly the skill every earlier topic in this group (reversal, fast/slow, merging) was building toward in isolation. These problems are the payoff round.

A good habit across all three: sketch the pointer state on paper (or verbally) before writing code, especially for the interleaving trick and the flattening splice — both have enough simultaneous pointer relationships that keeping them straight from memory alone is where mistakes creep in.

slides.sectionTitle: Where the rest of this pattern lives
slides.markdown:
Two closely related design problems deliberately live elsewhere so they aren't duplicated: the **LRU Cache**, whose ordering half is a doubly linked list identical in spirit to the ones in this group, is owned by the `hashing` group alongside the hashmap half of that design — the interesting part of LRU is really the combination, not the list alone.

And merging k sorted lists — which you've already seen solved with pairwise merging in the previous topic — has a heap-based alternative that trades constant factors differently; that version is covered in the `heaps` group's k-way merge topic.

Knowing where a pattern's *other* implementation lives, and why a curriculum splits it that way, is itself a useful interview instinct: it signals you see these as one underlying idea wearing different clothes, not as unrelated problems to memorize separately.
